narrative_idea_gen: A rooftop pigeon-racing club in Kensington, Philadelphia—six guys who've flown birds together for eleven years—falls apart when they vote out Teddy Morak for doctoring his birds with veterinary steroids, and Teddy, who has nothing else and no one else, refuses to disappear. Instead he begins a slow, petty siege on club president Carmine Deluca's daily life: showing up at his work, befriending his neighbors, registering a rival club one block over, poisoning every small comfortable routine Carmine has until the man can't buy a hoagie without looking over his shoulder. The whole thing is narrated by Milt Pfeiffer, the club's seventy-eight-year-old treasurer, who sits on his roof each evening tending his own birds and sees with painful clarity that Teddy isn't evil and Carmine isn't innocent—that both men are just lonely enough to destroy each other over the only community that ever made them feel like they belonged. It ends on a frozen January morning when Carmine's best bird lands on Teddy's roof by mistake, and the two men have to stand in Teddy's kitchen together for the first time in eight months, saying nothing, drinking coffee from the same dented percolator they used for a decade, while Milt watches from across the alley and thinks maybe that's close enough to forgiveness for guys like them.

narrative_beats:
# Seven Scene-Level Beats for the Kensington Pigeon Story

---

## Beat 1: The Vote on Teddy's Roof

**Concrete Action:** The six members of the rooftop pigeon-racing club gather on Carmine Deluca's roof on a late-May evening to vote on whether to expel Teddy Morak for doping his birds with veterinary anabolic steroids. Milt Pfeiffer, seventy-eight, club treasurer, narrates. The vote is 5–1 to expel. Teddy does not rage. He does not plead. He folds his lawn chair—his own chair, which he brought eleven years ago—and carries it down the roof stairs without a word. Milt watches him cross the alley below, chair under one arm, and notices Teddy doesn't go inside his own house. He just stands in his backyard holding the chair, as if waiting for someone to call him back. Nobody does. Milt tends his birds and says nothing.

**Narrative Technique — In Medias Res Through the Bystander's Eye:** Like the Baldwin model, the story drops us into the crisis before we have context. We don't yet know these men, their history, or why this club matters so desperately. But the craft decision that defines this story's entire architecture is the *point of view.* Milt is neither combatant. He is the treasurer, the oldest, the one who sits on his own roof across the alley and sees both men's houses. This is *triangulated first-person narration*—a witness positioned equidistant from two principals, able to see what neither can see about the other. The structural promise is built into the geometry: Milt's roof looks down on both Carmine's and Teddy's. He is literally above the conflict, which will become his moral problem—observation without intervention, clarity without courage.

The key image—Teddy standing in his yard holding a folded lawn chair, not going inside—should operate the way Baldwin's ice metaphor does: as a sensory detail that becomes a structural throughline. The chair is Teddy's membership, his seat at the table. He carries it out. He doesn't put it down. This image should recur or rhyme at the story's end.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The opening problem is not the cheating. It's the silence. Five men vote a sixth man out of the only thing that holds him to the world, and not one of them—including our narrator—says *stay.* Milt's failure to speak is the story's original sin, and it should be established here with zero editorializing. He watches. He notices the chair. He feeds his birds. The reader should feel the wrongness before Milt names it, because Milt may never fully name it. His guilt should live in what he *describes* rather than what he *confesses.*

---

## Beat 2: Milt Recounts the Eleven Years — How the Club Became the Only Country These Men Have

**Concrete Action:** In a passage that moves between summary and specific memory, Milt tells us how the club began: Carmine and Teddy started it together, two guys in their forties who met because their rooftops were close enough to watch each other's birds. Other men joined. Milt gives us the texture of eleven years—the weekend races, the Thursday-night record-keeping on Carmine's roof with beer and hoagies, the petty arguments about breed lines, the one time they pooled money to help Ray Brogan's wife with hospital bills. He catalogs what each man has outside the club: Carmine has an ex-wife in New Jersey and a part-time counter job; Teddy has a disability check and an empty rowhouse; Milt has a dead wife's African violets he still waters. The portrait is of six men for whom this small, regular gathering is the *entire social architecture* of their lives.

**Narrative Technique — Exposition as Elegy, Catalog as Characterization:** This beat does the work that Baldwin's mother's story does: it establishes *what is at stake* by revealing what came before. But the technique is different. Instead of a single embedded narrative, this should be a *mosaic of small memories*—a catalog structure where each detail is chosen for its ordinariness. The point is accumulation. No single memory is dramatic. But together they constitute a life. The reader should understand, by the end of this passage, that expelling Teddy from this club is not like firing someone or ending a friendship. It is closer to *exile.*

Milt's voice is critical here. He should narrate with the specificity of a man who has kept the books for eleven years—he remembers dates, tallies, which bird won which race in which year. His precision is his form of love. He counts because counting is how he holds on.

The key revelation, handled without emphasis, should be that Carmine and Teddy *co-founded* the club. This transforms the vote from a disciplinary action into a betrayal with a specific face. Carmine did not expel a member. He expelled his co-founder, the man who helped him build the only good thing in his life. This fact should be dropped into the catalog of memories without commentary and allowed to detonate quietly in the reader's mind.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The structural function is to make the reader *grieve the club before it's fully gone.* If this beat works, every subsequent scene of petty warfare will carry a double register: the absurdity of the escalation *and* the knowledge of what these routines replaced. The reader needs to feel the Thursday nights, the hoagies, the roof in summer. Without this, the story is just two stubborn men. With it, the story is about what happens when the last place you belong decides you don't.

---

## Beat 3: Teddy's Siege Begins — Small Infiltrations into Carmine's Daily Life

**Concrete Action:** Over the weeks following the vote, Teddy does not confront Carmine directly. Instead, he begins appearing in Carmine's routines. He starts buying his coffee at the same deli where Carmine goes every morning. He befriends Carmine's next-door neighbor and begins sitting on the neighbor's stoop in the evenings. He shows up at the hardware store where Carmine works part-time, not to make a scene but to buy something small—a pack of washers, a roll of tape—and be pleasant to the other employees. Each incursion is deniable. None is accidental. Milt learns about these episodes partly from Carmine, who complains with increasing agitation, and partly from his own observation. He watches from his roof as Teddy's patterns shift, orienting like a compass needle toward Carmine's life.

**Narrative Technique — Escalation Through Accumulation, the Unreliable Complaint, and Dual Surveillance:** The challenge of this beat is to render Teddy's campaign as simultaneously *menacing and pathetic,* never letting the reader settle into seeing him as either villain or victim. The technique is *catalytic accumulation*—a series of small, individually trivial actions that together create an unbearable pressure. Each incident should be narrated by Milt with a specific, concrete image. The effect is that of a list that keeps not ending.

Critically, Milt should receive this information through *two unreliable channels.* Carmine tells him about the encounters, but Carmine is increasingly paranoid, so the reader can't be sure which sightings are strategic and which are coincidental. Milt also observes some things directly from his roof, but rooftop observation is partial—he sees arrivals and departures, not conversations. This *epistemic limitation* should be built into the narration honestly. Milt should occasionally say he doesn't know what was said, or that he's guessing at Teddy's motive. This restraint builds trust with the reader and deepens the story's central theme: that we narrate other people's intentions from insufficient evidence, always.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The siege should feel like a *haunting* conducted by a living person. Teddy is not violent. He is *present.* And his presence is unbearable to Carmine precisely because it is a reminder—of the friendship, the betrayal, the vote. Baldwin's surrogate-character beat (the friend outside the school) works because the minor character is a *mirror.* Teddy functions the same way for Carmine: he is the visible proof that expulsion did not make the problem disappear. You cannot exile someone from a five-block radius. Kensington is too small. The neighborhood is the story's cage.

---

## Beat 4: Teddy Registers a Rival Club — The Formal Rupture

**Concrete Action:** Teddy registers a new pigeon-racing club with the local federation, based on his own rooftop, one block over. He recruits two younger guys from the neighborhood. He builds new loft structures visible from Carmine's roof. He begins racing under his own club's name. This is the action that transforms the conflict from personal to structural: Teddy is no longer just haunting Carmine; he is *replacing* him. Within the original club, the remaining members begin to fracture. Some think Carmine should talk to Teddy. Others think Teddy has lost his mind. Milt goes to a race where both clubs compete and watches from the parking lot as Carmine and Teddy stand thirty feet apart, neither acknowledging the other, both staring at the sky.

**Narrative Technique — The Mirror Structure and the Scene of Parallel Action:** The rival club is the story's structural midpoint and its most important architectural device. It creates a *doubling* that makes the conflict visible and spatial. Where before there was one club, now there are two. Where before there was one loft, now there are two sets of birds on neighboring rooftops. Baldwin's story about the father's brother works by revealing a *hidden repetition*—the narrator is reliving his father's loss. Here, the repetition is not hidden but *performed.* Teddy is deliberately constructing a mirror version of the thing he was expelled from. This is both revenge and longing: he is *rebuilding the community that rejected him,* which means he cannot let it go.

The race scene—both men staring at the sky, thirty feet apart—should be the beat's central image. Milt watches from a middle distance. The composition is triangular again: two men who won't look at each other, a third man who can't stop looking at both. The birds are above all of them. The sky is the only space they still share.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The rival club raises the story's stakes from emotional to existential. It asks: *Can you rebuild belonging from spite?* Teddy's new club is born from rejection, which means it carries rejection in its DNA. It will never be what the old club was, because the old club was built from affection and accident and Thursday nights. Teddy knows this. The reader should sense that he knows this. And yet he does it anyway, because the alternative is to do nothing, and doing nothing in an empty rowhouse is a form of death.

---

## Beat 5: Milt Visits Teddy's Kitchen — The View from Inside the Siege

**Concrete Action:** Milt, acting on no one's instructions, walks across the alley and knocks on Teddy's door. He has not been inside the house in months. Teddy lets him in. They sit in the kitchen with the dented percolator between them—the same one that used to come up to the roof on club nights. Teddy does not ask why Milt is there. They talk about birds, about the weather, about nothing. Then Teddy says something—one line, simple and unadorned—that reveals the depth of his loneliness. Maybe he mentions that he still sets out six mugs on Thursday nights before he remembers. Maybe he says the new guys don't know how to keep a book. Whatever it is, it should be *small and involuntary,* a confession that escapes through a crack in his composure. Milt does not respond with the right words. He finishes his coffee and leaves.

**Narrative Technique — The Failed Embassy and the Revealed Interior:** This beat corresponds structurally to Baldwin's Beat 5, the death of Grace—the moment when suffering becomes a *bridge* rather than a wall. But here, the bridge is only half-built. Milt crosses the alley, which is the most active thing he does in the entire story. He goes inside Teddy's loneliness and sees it up close: the kitchen, the percolator, the six mugs. But he does not convert that seeing into action. He does not mediate. He does not bring a message from Carmine. He goes home.

The structural function is dual. First, it gives the reader *direct access* to Teddy's interior, which has been visible only through Milt's rooftop surveillance and Carmine's paranoid reports. The kitchen is the first time we are inside Teddy's space, and every object should do characterizing work. Second, it establishes Milt's *complicity* as the story's quiet tragedy. He sees clearly. He understands both men. And he does nothing with that understanding. His narration after this scene should carry a faint, unspoken self-reproach—not guilt exactly, but the weariness of a man who knows he has failed at something he cannot name.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The detail of the six mugs—or whatever small domestic habit reveals that Teddy still lives inside a phantom version of the club—should be the most devastating image in the story. It must be delivered without sentimentality, in Milt's plain, ledger-keeping voice. The power comes from the *contrast* between the narrator's restraint and the enormity of what the detail reveals. If Milt weeps over it, the story collapses. If Milt simply notes it and moves on, the reader does the weeping.

---

## Beat 6: The Collapse of Small Routines — Winter Settles, Both Men Diminish

**Concrete Action:** As autumn turns to winter, the siege grinds on but loses its energy. Teddy's appearances in Carmine's routines become less frequent—not because he's relenting but because the cold keeps everyone indoors. The racing season is over. The birds are in their lofts. Carmine stops complaining to Milt, which is worse than complaining, because it means he has started to accept the new shape of his life. Milt observes from his roof—now wrapped in a coat, now staying shorter stretches—that both men's lights come on earlier and go off earlier. The neighborhood contracts in the cold. Milt tends his wife's African violets, which are struggling in the dry radiator heat. He thinks about what the club used to sound like in winter: the space heater on Carmine's roof, the thermoses, arguments about the spring race schedule.

**Narrative Technique — The Diminuendo, Negative Space, and the Objective Correlative of Seasonal Collapse:** This beat decelerates the story deliberately. The siege has peaked; what follows is not resolution but *entropy.* Baldwin's street-revival-singers beat works as a pivot from private pain to shared witness. This beat does something different: it creates a *silence* that the final scene must fill. The technique is one of *negative space*—describing what is not happening, who is not gathering, what the roof sounds like when no one is on it.

The African violets should function as Milt's objective correlative. They are his dead wife's. He keeps them alive. They are struggling. He cannot quite keep everything going. This should not be belabored—one or two sentences at most—but it should connect Milt to the story's deep theme: the fragile, daily, mostly-failing effort to keep alive the things that connect you to other people.

Seasonality is also structural. The story opened in late May. It will end in January. The full arc moves from warmth to cold, from open rooftops to closed kitchens. This is not symbolism imposed on the story;

# The Treasurer

The vote was on a Tuesday, the last one in May. We held it on Carmine's roof because that's where we always held things, up among the lofts with the evening settling pink over the rowhouse chimneys and the birds cooing in their boxes like they had opinions of their own. Carmine called it. He'd gotten the lab results back from Dr. Phan, the avian vet on Allegheny, and the numbers were right there on the printout: nandrolone metabolites in the urine of Teddy's cock bird, the blue-bar that had won three of the last five races by margins nobody could account for. Carmine read the numbers out loud. I remember that, because he read them the way you'd read a eulogy—steady, prepared, like he'd practiced it alone first.

There were six of us. Carmine Deluca. Teddy Morak. Ray Brogan. Dennis Mahler. Little Pete Stavros, who was six-foot-three but had been Little Pete since somebody's father gave him the name decades ago. And me. Milton Pfeiffer, treasurer, seventy-eight years old, keeper of the books since the second year.

Carmine said we'd do a hand vote. He said anyone who thought Teddy should be removed from the club should raise his hand.

Teddy was sitting in the lawn chair he'd brought up eleven years ago, the aluminum-frame one with the green and white webbing that had faded to green and gray. He had his hands on both armrests. He was looking at the birds.

Five hands went up. Carmine's, Ray's, Dennis's, Little Pete's, mine. Teddy did not raise his hand, obviously, but he also did not do any of the things I had spent the afternoon expecting. He didn't curse. He didn't throw the printout off the roof. He didn't say it was a mistake, a contamination, a conspiracy. He didn't say twenty-seven years of friendship should mean something. He didn't say any of the things that would have made it easier for the rest of us, because anger is easy to walk away from.

What he did was fold his lawn chair. He stood up, pressed the seat so the frame collapsed with that particular aluminum click, and tucked it under his arm. He nodded—not at anyone specifically, just a nod like he was confirming a figure in a column—and he went down the roof stairs. His footsteps on each plywood step. Then the back door opening and closing. Then nothing.

I was at the edge of the roof. I was always at the edge of the roof, because my own house is across the alley, and from Carmine's parapet I could see my lofts and check on my birds even during meetings. So I was the one who saw Teddy come out his back door into his yard. He still had the chair under his arm. He stopped in the middle of the concrete pad, between the rusted gas grill and the recycling bin. And he stood there. Just stood. Holding the folded chair like he was waiting at a bus stop, or like someone had told him to wait right there, they'd be back in a minute.

Nobody called down to him. Up on the roof Carmine was collecting the beer bottles and the printout, and the other three were muttering the way men mutter when they've done something necessary and don't want to think about whether it was right. I watched Teddy stand in his yard for what must have been four or five minutes. Then he went inside. But he took the chair with him. He didn't leave it in the yard where he kept his other outdoor things. He carried it into the house.

I went back to my roof that evening and fed my birds. Twenty-two homers in two lofts, all banded, all registered. I measured the feed the way I always do, three tablespoons per bird, a mix of peas, safflower, and red milo. The measuring is important. You overfeed a racing pigeon and the weight costs you seconds. You underfeed it and it won't home. I've been measuring for eleven years and I have never been off by more than a quarter tablespoon. This is not a boast. It is the only kind of discipline I have ever been able to maintain—the discipline of small things, done correctly, repeated.

On my way back inside I looked across the alley at Teddy's house. His kitchen light was on. That was all.

---

The club started in 2012, the year I turned sixty-seven. But it started without me. It started with Carmine and Teddy, two men in their mid-forties who happened to keep birds on rooftops close enough that they could see each other's lofts. I've heard the origin story from both of them, separately, and the versions agree on the essentials: Carmine was on his roof one April evening and saw a man on a roof one block over, handling a silver hen, and he yelled something across the gap—Carmine says it was "Nice bird," Teddy always said it was "Hey, that bird's too fat to race"—and the man yelled something back, and within a week they had walked the block between their houses and shaken hands in the alley and started talking about forming a club.

They registered with the American Racing Pigeon Union that June. Philadelphia Kensington Flyers. Carmine was president. Teddy was vice president and race secretary. Four months later I joined, because I had just retired from thirty-one years at the Frankford Candy Company, where I had kept the production ledgers, and my wife Ada had said I needed to do something outside the house before I drove her to murder. I brought my bookkeeping. They made me treasurer on the first Thursday.

Ray Brogan joined the following spring. Dennis Mahler in 2014. Little Pete in 2015. And that was it. Six men. You would think a club in a city this size could attract more, but pigeon racing is a dying sport. The old Italians and Poles and Irish who built lofts on every other rooftop in Kensington—those men are dead now, mostly, or in nursing homes in Bucks County. We were what was left.

I could tell you the winners of every race from 2012 to 2023. I have the books. I have the original books, the ones before we switched to the laptop in 2018, written in my hand in a series of composition notebooks—the black-and-white marbled kind, which I buy in bulk from the Dollar Tree on Frankford Avenue, eight at a time, because they are the correct size for a breast pocket. I have yards per minute, wind conditions, release coordinates, bird band numbers. I have the results from the day Ray's bird, a mealy hen called Duchess, set the club record in the two-hundred-mile race from Winchester, Virginia, at 1,847 yards per minute with a quartering headwind. I have the results from the day all six of us got skunked in the three-hundred-mile and none of our birds came home until the next morning, and we stood on Carmine's roof in the dark, listening, waiting for the sound of wings.

I have the expenses too. The Thursday-night accounting. We split the cost of race entry fees and fuel for the release trailer. I recorded them all. $14.50 per member for the Hagerstown race, April 2016. $22.00 per member for the series of five young-bird races, fall 2017, because fuel prices spiked. In 2019, when Ray's wife Helen needed surgery for her gallbladder and the insurance covered only part, the club voted unanimously to contribute two hundred dollars from the treasury plus whatever each man could give from his own pocket. The total was six hundred and forty dollars. I logged it as "Special Disbursement — Brogan Family" and I still have the receipt from the cashier's check.

These are the numbers. But the numbers are only the skeleton.

The body was the Thursday nights. May through October, every week, Carmine's roof. Lawn chairs in a half-circle facing the lofts. A cooler with Yuengling and, after Ray's doctor told him to quit drinking, a six-pack of Wawa iced tea. Hoagies from DiNic's if someone was feeling generous, or a bag of pretzels from the store if nobody was. I would read the prior week's figures. Carmine would assign training tosses. Teddy would argue about something—the band supplier, the feed mix, whether we should enter the Combine races or stick to our own schedule. Teddy argued about everything, not because he was disagreeable but because he could not help thinking, and thinking made him talk, and talking, for Teddy, was the same thing as arguing. He wasn't educated. He'd dropped out of Lincoln High in the eleventh grade. But he read—magazines, library books, things he found online—and he always came to Thursday nights with some theory about wing loading or immune supplements or the superiority of the Janssen bloodline, and he would hold the floor until Carmine told him to sit down, and then he would sit down, and then he would start again ten minutes later, and everyone would groan, and he would grin, and the evening would go on.

That was the body of it. The sound of Teddy talking and Carmine telling him to shut up and both of them laughing. The clink of bottles in the cooler. The birds settling into the lofts at dusk. Six men on a roof in Kensington, Pennsylvania, spending an evening together because there was nowhere else any of them particularly needed to be.

Carmine had an ex-wife in Cherry Hill. No kids. He worked three days a week at the Ace Hardware on Front Street. Teddy had been on disability since 2010, when his back gave out working the line at the old Budd Company plant—the plant was already closed by then, he was doing cleanup work for the demolition contractor, and something fell on him. He lived alone in a rowhouse he'd inherited from his mother. Ray was a retired mail carrier with bad knees. Dennis drove a school bus. Little Pete collected rent on two properties his father had left him and otherwise did nothing I could identify as employment. My own situation: retired, widowed since 2020, living in a house full of Ada's things. Her African violets on every windowsill. Twenty-three pots. I water them on a schedule—Tuesday and Saturday, with diluted fertilizer once a month—because they are alive, and the things that are alive require maintenance, and maintenance is something I know how to provide.

None of us had what you would call a full life. I say that without self-pity. You get to a certain age, or a certain set of circumstances, and the full life narrows to a few channels. The club was not a hobby. I want that to be clear. A hobby is something you could stop doing and the shape of your week would hold. The club was the shape.

I should say—I should mention, because it matters and because I did not give it appropriate weight at the time—that Teddy and Carmine started the club together. They co-founded it. They stood in the alley in 2012 and decided, together, to build something. Carmine designed the first lofts using plans from a book Teddy had checked out from the McPherson Square Library. Teddy drove to Gettysburg to pick up their foundation breeding pairs from an old Dutchman named Kreider who'd been racing since the Korean War. They shingled Carmine's roof access together, one holding the planks while the other nailed. This is all in the early books, before the formal entries began—just notes, really, in Carmine's handwriting and Teddy's, crammed into the margins of the first notebook.

I said I should mention it because it matters. I'll leave it at that.

---

The first incident was the coffee. This would have been mid-June, two, maybe three weeks after the vote. Carmine came up to my roof on a Saturday morning, which was unusual—Carmine did not come to my roof, I went to his—and he was holding a paper cup from the New Warsaw Deli on Belgrade Street.

"He was in there," Carmine said.

I asked who.

"Who do you think? Teddy. He's sitting at the counter eating a cheese Danish. Since when does Teddy go to the Warsaw? He lives eight blocks from the Warsaw. He goes to the Wawa on Aramingo like every other normal person."

I told Carmine that a man could buy coffee where he liked.

"He looked right at me, Milt. He didn't say a word. He just looked at me and chewed his Danish."

I said I didn't know what to tell him.

Carmine stood on my roof with his paper cup and stared across the alley at Teddy's house. The roof loft was visible from where we stood—Teddy hadn't taken his birds away after the vote, hadn't sold them or given them to anyone. They were up there cooing and strutting in the June sun. Carmine stared at them like they owed him money.

"He's doing it on purpose," Carmine said. "He wants me to know he's around."

I said maybe so.

The second incident was Mrs. Peralta's stoop. Gloria Peralta lived in the rowhouse adjacent to Carmine's on the east side. She was seventy, Dominican, church every morning, and she sat on her stoop in the evenings with a portable radio listening to the Phillies. Teddy, who had never to my knowledge exchanged more than a nod with Gloria Peralta in eleven years, began joining her. He brought his own chair—not the lawn chair from the roof, a different one, a folding camping chair—and sat beside her and listened to the game. Carmine told me about it in a voice I hadn't heard from him before, a voice with a seam in it.

"He's on Peralta's stoop, Milt. Every night. He's right there. I come out my front door and he's ten feet away listening to the goddamn Phillies."

"Does he talk to you?"

"He says hello. He says 'Hey, Carmine, how's it going.' Like nothing happened. Like he didn't pump his birds full of horse juice and get caught."

I watched from my roof one evening and confirmed it. Teddy was there on Gloria Peralta's stoop, kicked back in his camping chair. Carmine's front door was closed. Lights on inside. From above, the geometry was stark: Teddy positioned exactly where Carmine could not avoid him, planted in Carmine's periphery like a splinter.

Then the hardware store. Carmine told me Teddy came in on a Wednesday, bought a package of quarter-inch washers and a roll of plumber's tape, complimented the new girl at the register on her earrings, and left. Came back Friday. Bought a tube of caulk. Saturday, a paintbrush—a cheap one, the foam kind, a dollar twenty-nine. Each purchase totaling less than five dollars. Each time, according to Carmine, Teddy was friendly, pleasant, unrushed. He browsed. He asked about products. He treated the store like a place he had always come to and would always come to. Which, I should note, he had: Teddy had been buying things at that Ace Hardware for years before Carmine started working there. But he had never come three times in one week. That I could see.

I say "that I could see" because I want to be honest about what I know and what I am guessing. I am guessing about the washers and the caulk. Carmine told me those things, and by mid-July Carmine's accounts had taken on a quality I recognized from Ada's last years, when she would tell me the neighbor was watching her through the fence, or the pharmacist had given her the wrong pills on purpose. Not the same. Not that far. But a quality—a tightness, a certainty that everything was aimed at him.

Maybe it was. I don't know what was in Teddy's head. I know what I could see from a rooftop across an alley, which was arrivals and departures: what time Teddy left his house, which direction he walked, what time he came back. I could not see intentions. I could not hear what

Caribou Season at the Lodge
Genre: Surreal Horror

JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered.

The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way.

Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it.

JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes.  JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move.

And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse.

JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head.
